explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. While the enemy sat in the valley, the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon, Israel's leader (Judges 6:34). Right after that, Gideon blew the ram's horn and rallied the Abiezrites behind him. I think that's the best thing that can come upon a man when trouble moves in next door.

I get the guess, friend. With an army parked in the valley, a nap sounds like a fine idea to me. But the text says the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon, and then Gideon blew the ram's horn. Nobody is sleeping in this verse.

No sickness here, friend. The text says the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon (Judges 6:34). Then he blew the ram's horn and rallied the Abiezrites behind him. That sounds like a man who's up on his feet, and I bet nobody was checking his temperature.

Close, friend, but the text says more than that. Gideon did send messengers through Manasseh, and then it adds Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali. All of them came up to meet him (Judges 6:35). He sent that message a long way.
Right, friend, it's False. Gideon sent messengers throughout Manasseh, as well as Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali (Judges 6:35). Four places, not one. And the text says they came up to meet him.

explanations.answer: Dew only on the fleece and dry ground
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Gideon said, “If there is dew only on the fleece and all the ground is dry, then I will know that You are going to save Israel by my hand, as You have said.” (Judges 6:37) That's a very particular order for one night. Wet wool, dry floor.

explanations.answer: Fire to burn up the fleece by morning
explanations.explanation: Fire is a big ask, friend, and Gideon didn't ask for it. He asked for dew only on the fleece with all the ground dry (Judges 6:37). Nothing gets burned in this test. Honestly, nobody wants a burnt fleece, same as nobody wants a burnt batch.

explanations.answer: The fleece gone from the floor by dawn
explanations.explanation: Nope, the fleece stays right where it is. Gideon asks for dew only on the fleece, and for the ground to be dry (Judges 6:37). He plans to squeeze that fleece the next morning. A vanishing fleece wouldn't leave him much to squeeze.
You've got it, friend. Gideon squeezed the fleece and wrung out the dew, a bowlful of water (Judges 6:38). That's not a damp sock, that's a real amount. The fleece was SOAKED.

That's too small, friend. A few drops wouldn't need a bowl, and the text says Gideon wrung out a bowlful of water (Judges 6:38). The fleece held a lot. Think about squeezing out a full sponge, not just a dab.

That one belongs to the second night, friend. This morning, Gideon wrung out a bowlful of water from the fleece (Judges 6:38). The dry fleece comes after he asks again (Judges 6:39–40). Keep the nights straight and you're golden.

Yes, friend. After asking God not to be angry with him, Gideon asked for one more test (Judges 6:39). This time the fleece would be dry and the ground covered with dew. He turned it around from the first night.

It's actually True, friend. Gideon said, “Do not be angry with me; let me speak one more time.” (Judges 6:39) Then he asked for the fleece to be dry and the ground covered with dew. That's the reverse of the first night.

Not quite, friend. The LORD said the opposite: “You have too many men for Me to deliver Midian into their hands…” (Judges 7:2). Too many, not too few. That's a strange complaint for a man about to face an army.
Right, it's False. The LORD told Gideon, “You have too many men for Me to deliver Midian into their hands…” (Judges 7:2). The army wasn't too small, it was too big. Most generals never hear that one.

explanations.answer: So Israel won't say their own hand saved them
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The LORD said there were too many men “…lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” (Judges 7:2) He wanted no doubt about who delivered them. The credit belongs where it belongs.

explanations.answer: So Midian won't see them coming from far off
explanations.explanation: That's a smart battle idea, friend, but it isn't what the LORD said. He gave this reason: “…lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” (Judges 7:2) Spotting them from a distance never comes up. It's all about who gets the credit.

explanations.answer: So the march to the valley will go faster
explanations.explanation: A faster march would be nice, friend. Nobody likes a slow line. But the LORD's reason was “…lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” (Judges 7:2) Speed isn't mentioned in this verse.
Yes, friend. Gideon announced that whoever was fearful and trembling could turn back, and twenty-two thousand did (Judges 7:3). Only ten thousand stayed. That's most of the army walking home.

Somebody in that crowd was ready to head out, friend. The text says twenty-two thousand turned back, but ten thousand remained (Judges 7:3). That's far from none. It's a lot of people with the same thought.
A few is a small crowd, friend, and this wasn't small. Twenty-two thousand turned back, and only ten thousand remained (Judges 7:3). That's more than half of them walking away. Think MOST, not few.

explanations.answer: By how each man drinks the water
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The LORD told Gideon, “Separate those who lap the water with their tongues like a dog from those who kneel to drink.” (Judges 7:5) The test was the way each man drank. Nobody got a warning that this was a test, I bet.

explanations.answer: By who can carry the most water
explanations.explanation: Nobody's hauling buckets here, friend. The LORD had Gideon separate the men by how they drank: those who lap with their tongues and those who kneel (Judges 7:5). Carrying water never comes up. It was all about how they drank.

explanations.answer: By who crosses the water first
explanations.explanation: No race at the water, friend. The LORD told Gideon to separate those who lap the water from those who kneel to drink (Judges 7:5). It was about how a man drinks. Nobody's racing across anything.

That's it, friend. The number who lapped with their hands to their mouths was three hundred men, and all the others knelt to drink (Judges 7:6). Out of ten thousand, that's a tiny crew. And the LORD planned to use them.

That's ten times too many, friend. The text says the men who lapped with their hands to their mouths numbered three hundred (Judges 7:6). All the others knelt to drink. Three hundred is a small group, believe it or not.
Still too high, friend. The number who lapped the water with their hands to their mouths was three hundred (Judges 7:6). All the others knelt to drink. That's a very small slice of ten thousand.

That's right, friend. The LORD said, “With the three hundred men who lapped the water I will save you and deliver the Midianites into your hand.” (Judges 7:7) Three hundred men, and the LORD says He'll do the saving. That's a promise worth hearing.

Tests were happening, friend. The LORD said He would sift the men at the water (Judges 7:4). But in this verse He says, “With the three hundred men who lapped the water I will save you…” (Judges 7:7). The word here is save.

Fair guess, friend, but that word isn't in this verse. The LORD said, “With the three hundred men who lapped the water I will save you and deliver the Midianites into your hand.” (Judges 7:7) The word is save. He's making a promise, not giving a lesson.

explanations.answer: Take his servant and listen in on the camp
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. The LORD said, “…go down to the camp with your servant Purah and listen to what they are saying.” (Judges 7:10–11) Then Gideon's hands would be strengthened to attack the camp. The LORD gave him a way to go down and hear for himself.

explanations.answer: Call back the men who went home
explanations.explanation: Those men are staying home, friend. The LORD had sent the rest of them to their tents (Judges 7:8). His other option was to go down to the camp with his servant Purah and listen to what they were saying (Judges 7:10–11). Nobody gets called back.

explanations.answer: Send in the three hundred without him
explanations.explanation: Gideon doesn't hide behind his men, friend. The LORD told him to go down to the camp with his servant Purah and listen to what they were saying (Judges 7:10–11). Then his hands would be strengthened to attack. Nobody gets sent in ahead of him.

That's the one, friend. The man said, “…I saw a loaf of barley bread come tumbling into the Midianite camp.” (Judges 7:13) Yes, bread. Of all the things to see in a dream, a rolling loaf is quite the pick.

explanations.answer: A great stone from the hills
explanations.explanation: A stone would make sense for knocking over a tent, friend. But the man said he saw a loaf of barley bread come tumbling into the Midianite camp (Judges 7:13). It's bread, plain and simple. Nobody guessed that, and that's why it's memorable.

explanations.answer: A wild ox from the fields
explanations.explanation: An ox would do some damage, friend. But the man said he saw a loaf of barley bread tumbling into the camp (Judges 7:13). That's what hit the tent. I'd have lost sleep over that dream, honestly.

explanations.answer: God has given Midian to Gideon
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The friend said, “…God has delivered Midian and the whole camp into his hand.” (Judges 7:14) He called the loaf the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. And Gideon was standing right there, listening.

explanations.answer: Their camp will run out of water
explanations.explanation: Water isn't part of the interpretation, friend. The friend said the dream was the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite, and that God had delivered Midian and the whole camp into his hand (Judges 7:14). Nothing about wells or water. It's all about Gideon.

explanations.answer: A storm will hit the valley tonight
explanations.explanation: The weather forecast is clear, friend. The man's friend said the dream was the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite (Judges 7:14). God had delivered Midian and the whole camp into Gideon's hand. No storm in sight.
Yes, friend. When Gideon heard the dream and its interpretation, he bowed in worship (Judges 7:15). Then he went back to the camp of Israel. He worshiped first and moved second.
It's True, friend. When Gideon heard the dream and its interpretation, he bowed in worship (Judges 7:15). Only after that did he go back to the camp of Israel. Worship came first.

That's right, friend. Each man got a ram's horn in one hand and a large jar in the other, and inside the jar was a torch (Judges 7:16). Nobody in that valley could see a thing coming. A jar full of light is a good trick.

The swords come up later, friend, but they aren't in the jars. The text says each man held a large jar with a torch inside (Judges 7:16). In the other hand he held a ram's horn. It's an odd set of tools for a battle.

No reading material tonight, friend. The text says each man had a ram's horn in one hand and a large jar in the other, and inside the jar was a torch (Judges 7:16). Nobody's reading anything in the dark.
It's the other way around, friend. Gideon said, “Watch me and do as I do,” and, “…do exactly as I do.” (Judges 7:17) He wasn't staying behind. He goes with them, and the men follow his lead.

That's right, friend. Gideon told them, “Watch me and do as I do,” and, “…do exactly as I do.” (Judges 7:17) That doesn't sound like a man staying behind. The text says Gideon and the hundred men with him reached the outskirts of the camp (Judges 7:19).

explanations.answer: For the LORD and for Gideon
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Gideon told them, “…shout, ‘For the LORD and for Gideon!’” (Judges 7:18) When the moment came, they shouted, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” (Judges 7:20). The LORD comes first in the cry.

That's a nice battle cry, friend, but it isn't the one Gideon gave. He told them to shout, “For the LORD and for Gideon!” (Judges 7:18) Israel and Manasseh aren't in the line. The LORD is named first.

explanations.answer: For our land and our people
explanations.explanation: That's a fine cry, friend, but it isn't the one in the text. Gideon said, “…shout, ‘For the LORD and for Gideon!’” (Judges 7:18) No land, no people in the line. Just the LORD and Gideon.

That's right, friend. Gideon and the hundred men with him blew their horns and broke the jars that were in their hands (Judges 7:19). The other two companies shattered theirs too (Judges 7:20). The jars were hiding the torches, so the breaking let the torchlight out.

Nobody's digging, friend. The text says they blew their horns and broke the jars in their hands (Judges 7:19). The torches had been inside, and the breaking set them free. Burying them would have kept the light hidden.

Nobody's throwing anything, friend. The text says Gideon's men broke the jars that were in their hands (Judges 7:19). They held the torches in their left hands and the horns in their right hands (Judges 7:20). The jars broke right where they were standing.
Not quite, friend. The text says each Israelite took his position around the camp (Judges 7:21). They stayed on the outside. Nobody charged into the middle.
Right, it's False. Each Israelite took his position around the camp (Judges 7:21). They held the outskirts and made their noise from there. And the entire Midianite army fled anyway.
Yes, friend. The entire Midianite army fled, crying out as they ran (Judges 7:21). That's an army that had just heard three hundred horns. I think nobody stopped to ask what was going on.
It's True, friend. The text says the entire Midianite army fled, crying out as they ran (Judges 7:21). Every one of them took off. That's an entire army, not just a few.

explanations.answer: Turns the men against one another
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. When the three hundred rams' horns sounded, the LORD set all the men in the camp against one another with their swords (Judges 7:22). The three hundred didn't have to fight their way in. The LORD did the work.

explanations.answer: Sends hail down on their tents
explanations.explanation: No hail in this story, friend. The text says the LORD set all the men in the camp against one another with their swords (Judges 7:22). It happened as the rams' horns sounded. The fight was among the Midianites themselves.

The camels were there, friend, as countless as the sand on the seashore (Judges 7:12). But this verse doesn't say they stampeded. It says the LORD set all the men in the camp against one another with their swords (Judges 7:22).

You got it, friend. Gideon told the men of Ephraim to “…seize the waters of the Jordan ahead of them as far as Beth-barah.” (Judges 7:24) And they did just that. They got ahead of the Midianites and held the water.

Close to home, but not this one, friend. The Kishon isn't mentioned in this passage. Gideon's call to Ephraim was to “…seize the waters of the Jordan ahead of them as far as Beth-barah.” (Judges 7:24) The Jordan is the one.

The Nile is a long way off, friend. Gideon's message to the men of Ephraim was to “…seize the waters of the Jordan ahead of them as far as Beth-barah.” (Judges 7:24) The Nile never comes up in this story. I'd need a very long road to get there.

explanations.answer: On the other side of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The men of Ephraim brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian, to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan (Judges 7:25). They pursued the Midianites all the way across. Gideon was waiting out there.

explanations.answer: Back at his home in Ophrah
explanations.explanation: Gideon isn't home, friend. The text says the men of Ephraim brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan (Judges 7:25). Ophrah isn't mentioned in this passage. He was still out in the thick of it.

explanations.answer: In the hill country of Ephraim
explanations.explanation: That's where Gideon sent his messengers, friend (Judges 7:24). But the text says the men of Ephraim brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan (Judges 7:25). So Gideon was across the river.
